journal_name: New Zealand Journal of Educational Studies
title: Reflexivity as Epistemological Imperative: An Autoethnographic Account of Researching Indian Diaspora Youth in Aotearoa New Zealand
abstract: Abstract This paper argues that, in contexts characterised by diversity and cultural complexity, such as those of diaspora scholarship, reflexivity becomes indispensable for producing ethically sound and contextually grounded knowledge. Through autoethnographic analysis of my doctoral research journey investigating the aspirations of Indian-identifying youth (ages 18–25) in Aotearoa New Zealand, I use shifting decisions about research approach and positionality as illustrative cases for theorising reflexivity’s epistemological, methodological, and ethical functions. Rather than treating reflexivity as merely methodological enhancement, I conceptualise researcher reflection as an epistemological necessity specific to diaspora research contexts, where fluid identities, complex power dynamics, and heterogeneous migration histories demand continuous critical engagement with positionality. title: Transdisciplinary research to address youth vaping in Aotearoa New Zealand
abstract: Abstract Transdisciplinary educational approaches are increasingly being used to prepare students to address complex societal challenges that extend beyond traditional disciplinary boundaries. This paper describes a pilot programme at the University of Auckland that embedded transdisciplinary research into undergraduate education, drawing on principles from the Vertically Integrated Project (VIP) model as a proof-of-concept pedagogical initiative. Youth vaping is a growing public health challenge in Aotearoa New Zealand, providing an authentic context through which to explore this educational approach. Over ten weeks, six undergraduate University students from Public Health, Education, and Engineering disciplines collaborated to synthesise evidence, explore disciplinary perspectives, and co-design strategies to reduce youth vaping. Activities included literature reviews, data scraping for surveillance research, and a final solutions project presented as research posters and a stakeholder pitch. title: Being a White Tauiwi, a Tangata Tiriti, and a Researcher in Aotearoa
abstract: Abstract This article examines how the author’s positionality as a white tauiwi (non-Māori, non-Pacific), tangata Tiriti, doctoral researcher has been continually reconfigured while conducting research with Māori and Pacific young people in Aotearoa New Zealand. Situated within a critical ethnographic approach informed by the practice of wayfinding, the article argues that researcher positionality is not established through a single declaration of reflexivity but is continually negotiated through relationality, reciprocity, and ongoing critical reflexivity. Rather than presenting discomfort as an obstacle to research, it argues that productive discomfort constitutes an ethical orientation that enables non-Indigenous researchers to remain accountable to Indigenous self-determination while recognising the limits of their own knowledge and authority. Drawing on personal narrative, theoretical reflection, and methodological analysis, the article traces how engagement with Te Tiriti o Waitangi, Māori and Pacific scholarship, and Indigenous onto-epistemologies transformed both the author’s understanding of herself as a French settler in Turtle Island Canada and the design of her doctoral

journal_name: New Zealand Journal of Educational Studies
title: High Aspiration Māori Students Experience of Secondary School
abstract: Abstract This study examines the English-medium secondary school experiences of 12 Māori students who identified themselves as having high aspirations and clear goals for further education. Data were collected through individual interviews with seven students and a focus group involving five students. Participants were asked to reflect on the practices of teachers and school leaders that supported their aspirations, as well as the extent to which school policies and practices enabled their goal setting, career decision-making, and academic progress. Students consistently described how teachers demonstrated high expectations and care in supporting their learning needs. They also provided insights into school-based processes, including goal-setting practices and subject selection mechanisms. Participants identified key school and department-level factors that supported their success, while also acknowledging the negative effects of racism on their educational experiences. journal_name: New Zealand Journal of Educational Studies
title: A Life Story Board approach to understanding the educational experiences of tauira Māori in sciences: A Pilot Study
abstract: Abstract There is an urgent need to improve support and teaching initiatives for tauira Māori studying sciences at university, and it is valuable to learn from the success stories of tauira who are persevering despite adversity. Underpinned by kaupapa Māori principles, we developed a culturally rich storytelling approach incorporating the Life Story Board (a visual qualitative research tool) led to explore the experiences of tauira Māori studying sciences, This approach was piloted by two Māori student researchers in peer-led storyboarding sessions. We conducted follow-up interviews ( n = 4) with participants to explore the impacts of the LSB method. We found that the storyboarding approach fostered trust between peer-interviewers and participants, and enabled mutual sharing of lived experiences from a strengths-based standpoint that uplifted the mana of all parties. This novel, culturally-immersive storyboarding approach shows exciting promise for future studies aimed at understanding experiences of tauira Māori and other historically marginalised groups.

journal_name: New Zealand Journal of Educational Studies
title: A Cyclopedia of Girls and Physical Education
abstract: Abstract This article experiments with form to offer readers a sense of girls’ experiences of physical education in Aotearoa New Zealand. Inspired by Rebecca Solnit’s (2014) Cyclopedia of an Arctic Expedition , and theoretical ideas from new materialisms and postqualitative inquiry, we assemble an alphabetised cyclopedia of participant comments that evoke varied scenes and sensations. Rather than arranging girls’ comments into stable themes that develop a cohesive argument, the cyclopedia functions more as an invitation to an encounter where meaning emerges relationally in the act of reading. Reading is conceptualised as an ‘event’ that is open-ended, where impressions always become anew. The cyclopedia begins with a preface to set the scene, and concludes with an afterword that provides further methodological context for the reader.

journal_name: New Zealand Journal of Educational Studies
title: Relationships with Mathematics: A Broad Construct for Understanding Mathematical Affect and Identity
abstract: Abstract The relationships with mathematics construct provides a framework for understanding the complex ways students engage with, learn, and participate in mathematics. This paper examines the construct, drawing on a longitudinal study of 31 secondary students in New Zealand. The study identified five interrelated elements that comprise students’ relationships with mathematics: beliefs about mathematics, mathematical knowledge, macro-feelings, perceptions of mathematical capabilities, and habits of engagement. Findings show that these elements were highly interconnected and evolved over time as students participated in mathematics classrooms and interpreted their experiences. Students’ relationships with mathematics shaped their engagement with mathematical tasks, their affective responses to challenge and success, and their ongoing participation in the subject. The construct highlights the dynamic interplay between cognitive, affective, identity-related, and social dimensions of mathematical learning and helps explain why students respond differently to similar mathematical experiences. journal_name: New Zealand Journal of Educational Studies
title: Mathematics Slash Pāngarau or Mathematics and Pāngarau
abstract: Abstract In this article, we challenge the dominant understanding in New Zealand education of the term pāngarau as curriculum mathematics translated into te reo Māori, (the Māori language). This is commonly expressed using the conjoined term mathematics/pāngarau implying that the two terms are equivalent and interchangeable. We outline a number of critiques of this situation from epistemological, language/power and ethnomathematical perspectives. We also discuss how the term mathematics/pāngarau generates struggle through various toxic effects in kura Māori (Māori schools) in terms of legitimation and the focus of education using research data. We conclude by proposing that pāngarau is already showing signs of emerging as a distinct entity in its own right and that this emergence should be accelerated so we begin to talk about mathematics and pāngarau rather than mathematics/pāngarau.

journal_name: New Zealand Journal of Educational Studies
title: Early Childhood Education Practice on the Edge: How Beginner Teachers from Migrant Backgrounds Negotiate and Understand Risk in Aotearoa New Zealand
abstract: Abstract As Aotearoa New Zealand’s early childhood education (ECE) sector becomes increasingly shaped by transnational mobility, migrant teachers are required to negotiate culturally embedded understandings of childhood, learning, and risk within locally situated pedagogical and regulatory frameworks. This paper explores how beginner ECE teachers from migrant backgrounds understand and negotiate children’s engagement with risk, and what these negotiations reveal about professional identity formation and transnational pedagogical adaptation. Drawing on qualitative narrative inquiry with twelve recently graduated migrant teachers working in Aotearoa New Zealand, the study applies the concept of edgework to examine how teachers balance safety, accountability, and pedagogical responsibility. Findings indicate that participants’ early approaches to risk were strongly influenced by prior educational experiences that positioned children as vulnerable and in need of protection. Over time, engagement with sociocultural pedagogies that position children as competent and capable prompted changes in participants’ professional beliefs and practices. journal_name: New Zealand Journal of Educational Studies
title: The Recontextualisation of Key Competencies in New Zealand and China: A Case Study from Chemistry
abstract: Abstract The 2007 New Zealand Curriculum was considered world-leading when it emerged with its new emphasis on generic key competencies. It was underpinned by a student-centred, future-focused narrative aiming to contribute to developing the knowledge and skills students would need to succeed as economically productive citizens in a new global economy. However, recent reforms indicate a shift away from generic competencies towards greater knowledge content specification. This move away from key competencies is interesting within the context of a China/New Zealand comparison, given that the Chinese educational context appears to be moving away from a ‘traditional’ content driven approach to education towards incorporating some 21st-century learning ideas, including key competencies and promotion of learner-centred pedagogies. Firstly, we provide a brief overview of the emergence of key competencies in New Zealand and then we compare that with their emergence in China including the development of what we term ‘subject’ key competencies. title: STEM and Migrant Students—On Becoming a New Zealander
abstract: Abstract This article reports on a small research project which explored the role that STEM education can play in the process of migrant students endeavouring to find a place in New Zealand society. An innovative methodology was used, drawing on data collected from stimulated-recall focus groups after students engaged with learning activities, which were situated within their current learning context. In total, 16 migrant students from Year 11, 12, and 13 years took part in this study. Data were analysed thematically, and this process showed that STEM educational experiences are relatively unimportant for these migrant students who were more concerned with a pragmatic approach that sought to find the most lucrative or appropriate career choice to have a prosperous life in New Zealand. Important issues were raised about the interplay between stereotypical views of STEM and New Zealand, and the contextualised, sophisticated understandings students also carried from their own lived experiences. journal_name: New Zealand Journal of Educational Studies
title: Effective and Inclusive Teaching for Young People from Refugee Backgrounds: An Appreciative Inquiry
abstract: Abstract Education in resettlement contexts offers a pathway to employment, civic integration and a sense of normalcy for former refugees. In Aotearoa New Zealand (NZ), resettlement policy prioritises education as a pathway to participation and belonging, but educational support for resettled refugees is limited. For students from refugee backgrounds, educational access and outcomes are often dependent on the will and expertise of teachers and school leaders, as well as students’ own self-sufficiency. In this paper, we outline the findings of an “appreciative inquiry” with primary and secondary teachers and school leaders who were identified as effective and inclusive by young people, families, and educational support staff from migrant and refugee backgrounds. We sought to identify the everyday ways in which teachers and schools fostered learning and belonging for students from refugee backgrounds. journal_name: New Zealand Journal of Educational Studies
title: Learning Progressions: A Novel Tool for Planning, Teaching and Assessing in Science Education
abstract: Abstract Change is a constant factor in education. Curricula are refreshed to reflect the educational outcomes required in a rapidly changing society and pedagogies evolve in response to new insights into how children learn. In this constantly changing environment, teachers embark upon a career-long cycle of professional learning and development. Most primary school teachers in New Zealand are generalist teachers and therefore face the task of remaining up to date with the latest changes across a range of subjects. Some of these changes come with the support of ‘off-the-peg’ resources, such as programmes that can be purchased by schools to implement structured literacy in schools. However, in this paper we focus on the potential of learning progressions (LPs) to support non-science specialist teachers when planning, teaching and assessing children’s understanding of scientific concepts. We detail the development of an LP for the understanding of a science concept pertinent to New Zealand’s endemic species. journal_name: New Zealand Journal of Educational Studies
title: Using a Bioecological Proximal Process Model to Understand Tensions in Teacher Identity Development
abstract: Abstract The development of a strong professional teacher identity plays an important role in supporting early career teacher development and teacher career longevity. The ways in which tensions between personal and professional identities are experienced and managed by preservice teachers (PSTs) can influence the development of teacher identity. This study explores how PSTs manage tensions they encounter in the development of their professional teacher identity. The study data are eight focus group discussions with a total of 24 PSTs who were near the end of their first year of a three-year, undergraduate, university-based initial teacher education (ITE) programme in New Zealand. Using Bronfenbrenner’s bioecological model of development, with particular attention to the interactions among proximal processes embedded within the model, the study finds that the features of self, development outcomes, context, and time are key elements of managing tensions in identity development. The PSTs also experienced these tensions across layers of the bioecological model and worked at the interface of these layers to manage the tensions. journal_name: New Zealand Journal of Educational Studies
title: Toward Te Tiriti Consciousness in Health Education
abstract: Abstract This article contributes to the emerging scholarship on Te Tiriti o Waitangi-led education by theorising the early formation of Te Tiriti consciousness - a contextually specific form of critical consciousness grounded in tino rangatiratanga (Māori authority and self-determination) in Aotearoa New Zealand. Drawing on reflexive thematic analysis of 106 written reflections from first-year public health students, the study explores how learners engage with Te Tiriti content and its implications for professional identity. Three interrelated themes trace students’ transformative learning trajectories: confronting structured ignorance, navigating identity disruption, and reorienting professional purpose. Students described the shock of discovering hidden histories, the emotional labour of reckoning with complicity, and an emerging sense of responsibility to uphold Te Tiriti in practice. We argue that Te Tiriti consciousness extends Freirean conscientisation by grounding critical consciousness in tino rangatiratanga and by being emotionally and relationally mediated through whanaungatanga (relational accountability). journal_name: New Zealand Journal of Educational Studies
title: The Philosophical Dimensions of Pākehā Positionality: Implications for Teaching in Secondary Schools in Aotearoa New Zealand
abstract: Abstract Secondary school teachers in Aotearoa New Zealand are accountable to the 2026 Standards for the Teaching Profession , which centre on Te Tiriti o Waitangi partnership. In its current form, the standards seem to expect a form of cultural competency from teachers that ignores the colonial foundations of schooling. This paper explores how Pākehā teachers, rather than attempting cultural competency, can strengthen our anticolonial literacy by attending to positionality. Pākehā positionality—in and beyond education contexts—has been widely discussed, but few texts have explicitly considered the philosophical assumptions inherent in positionality and how teachers’ self-awareness of these assumptions can bolster a commitment to Te Tiriti. Drawing from Indigenous and decolonial theories, I offer a conceptual analysis of settler ontological and epistemological assumptions and their relationship to schooling. Inspired by the metaphors of itulagi (Vaai & Casimira, 2017) and the triangulation of meaning (Meyer, 2008), I offer two sets of reflexive questions for Pākehā teachers to gauge how our enacted philosophical assumptions perpetuate or disrupt coloniality in the classroom. journal_name: New Zealand Journal of Educational Studies
title: Simplism in Education or Why ‘Rocket Science’ Isn’t a Good Analogy
abstract: Abstract Teaching, learning and wider educational systems entail complex activities. Claiming that a set of detailed prescriptions based on selective principles from educational sciences is all that is required to be effective, is simplism, it misunderstands the nature of that complexity. However, policies and practices can be, and are being enacted which require greater prescription and more structured universal programmes than we have had in Aotearoa New Zealand. Under some conditions, these may provide needed resources, but they carry significant risks for meeting our excellence and equity goals. This paper discusses the nature of the complexity and what educational sciences indicate about principles underlying effective teaching, learning and system change. It outlines the risks in simplifying and prescribing, and what enables innovation and flexibility with that complexity. Our phenomena are not like ‘rocket science’ and certainly not simpler, although some policies and practices can make what we do a limited form of technical expertise.

title: Navigating the Unknown: Educator Perspectives on Transnational Higher Education in Aotearoa
abstract: Abstract Transnational higher education is increasing around the globe as well as in Aotearoa New Zealand. Despite this, TNHE remains largely overlooked by the New Zealand government, leaving institutions to develop their own approaches. At the same time, existing TNHE research overwhelmingly focuses on the management and administration of TNHE, at the expense of understanding the reality on the ground. For this reason, this research aims to understand the lived experiences and perspectives of TNHE educators teaching on behalf of New Zealand higher education institutions. Through unstructured in-depth interviews grounded in a phenomenological approach with 11 interviewees across five institutions, this research enabled educators to discuss what they thought was most salient about their experiences and perspectives. Interviews were thematically analysed to find common themes and meanings across their experiences. The findings demonstrate that educators largely feel uncertain about and unprepared for their TNHE teaching, and have to navigate the challenges of teaching across multiple countries and academic systems through a process of trial-and-error. title: Exploring Specialist Resource Teachers’ Intentions to Implement Evidence-Based Practice: Indications Based on the Theory of Planned Behaviour
abstract: Abstract Sustainable Development Goal 4 (SDG 4)—one of the 17 Sustainable Development Goals adopted by the United Nations to address major global challenges by 2030—aims to ensure inclusive and equitable quality education and promote lifelong learning opportunities for all. Evidence‑based practice (EBP) is closely aligned with this goal because it enhances the capacity of education systems to provide inclusive, equitable, and effective learning for all children and young people. Given this connection, there is a global focus on promoting EBP as countries work towards achieving SDG 4. Despite the emphasis on the importance of EBP in education, there is limited research examining educators’ implementation of EBP in their daily practice. Responding to this gap in the research, the present study applies the Theory of Planned Behaviour (TPB) to explore Specialist Resource Teachers’ (SRTs) intentions to implement EBP and the factors that influence their implementation of EBP. Quantitative and qualitative data were gathered from 84 SRTs in Aotearoa New Zealand via an online questionnaire. journal_name: New Zealand Journal of Educational Studies
title: Building Futures: Engaging Students with Dioramas in STEAM Education
abstract: Abstract This study examined the perspectives and experiences of teachers and students in constructing dioramas. It was conducted in a small rural secondary school in Aotearoa, New Zealand. The three-dimensional models acted as tools for helping students visualise and represent ideas, supporting the development of environmental and sustainability concepts. The study involved four teachers collaboratively teaching a combined Year 9 and 10 class within an integrated STEAM (Science, Technology, Environment, Arts, Mathematics) programme, where students were challenged to design and construct imaginary habitats of future homes and local environments as dioramas, merging scientific knowledge with creative expression. The purpose of using dioramas extended beyond artistic representation; they provided a tangible way for students to engage with climate science by modelling ecosystems, illustrating interdependencies, and simulating the impact of human actions on environments. Through this process, students explored cause-and-effect relationships, considered adaptation and mitigation strategies, and envisioned sustainable futures. journal_name: New Zealand Journal of Educational Studies
title: Rethinking Philosophy Education in Aotearoa’s New Curriculum Through Plato’s Academy
abstract: Abstract The forthcoming inclusion of philosophy in Aotearoa New Zealand’s secondary school curriculum presents a timely opportunity to rethink how philosophy should be taught. This paper argues that philosophy education must move beyond the standardised and overly academic models often found in universities, which risk reducing the discipline to technical exercises rather than meaningful inquiry. Returning to the dialogical and imaginative spirit of Plato’s Academy, the paper advocates for teaching practices that prioritise dialogue, curiosity, and creativity over rote instruction and rigid assessment. Drawing on experimental teaching methods developed in collaboration with a university colleague and on practical experiences teaching philosophy at a secondary school in New Zealand, it demonstrates how dialogical and creative assessments, such as student-written dialogues and role-based discussions, enhance engagement and deepen philosophical understanding. journal_name: New Zealand Journal of Educational Studies
title: From Worldviews to Transformation: Staff Epistemologies and Institutional Change in an Aotearoa New Zealand Science Centre
abstract: Abstract This study investigates the epistemological, pedagogical, and cultural frameworks that guided the redevelopment of Tūhura Otago Community Trust Science Centre, a major science centre in Aotearoa New Zealand. Through semi-structured interviews with floor staff and museum decision makers conducted before and after the transformation, the study explores staff ideas regarding science, science communication and how their worldviews shaped exhibit design, institutional philosophy, and public engagement strategies. Findings reveal that staff held diverse epistemological views, though most framed science as an instrument or method for generating knowledge, with floor staff showing a broader and more inquiry-oriented epistemology than decision makers. Furthermore, emotional engagement, intergenerational learning and authenticity in exhibit interaction emerged as key elements of science communication. The study also examines the integration of Mātauranga Māori—including Indigenous Māori knowledge—as a partner epistemological framework, representing a significant shift towards bicultural science communication. journal_name: New Zealand Journal of Educational Studies
title: Careful Change, or Rash Reform: What Next for NCEA?
abstract: Abstract When New Zealand’s government proposed replacing the National Certificate of Educational Achievement (NCEA) in August 2025 after a six-week consultation, what did this urgency reveal about contemporary educational governance? This article asks what remains unexamined in the rush to reform: whose evidence counts as legitimate, whose voices matter in educational decision-making, and what remains of ‘equity’ when government acknowledges that its proposed reforms will cause harm to already disadvantaged groups of students? This article does not argue for or against the replacement of NCEA. Rather, drawing on the concept of moral panic, together with Ball’s critical policy discourse analysis and scholarship on neoliberal educational reform, we set out to formulate and discuss three main questions about the proposal. Our analyses uncover trends indicating that the reforms are motivated and shaped by ideological loyalty to standardisation, managerial oversight, and market responsiveness, rather than by careful consideration of all available educational evidence. journal_name: New Zealand Journal of Educational Studies
title: Versions and Visions: A (New) National English Curriculum for Aotearoa New Zealand
abstract: Abstract The recent English (national) curriculum change process in Aotearoa New Zealand has been an extraordinary episode in English curriculum history and indeed in curriculum inquiry more generally. Two such major policy documents in little over two years represents an exemplary instance of English curriculum politics. This paper provides an account of this episode from an ‘outsider’ perspective: the point of view of an English curriculum scholar from outside New Zealand. It reviews the change process in the period at issue, and the challenge of changing English in New Zealand, and considers this with reference to the knowledge debate in English teaching more broadly. It also seeks to analyse the specific role and significance of Elizabeth Rata in this regard, as a central figure in the episode, and indeed a ‘primary definer’. The paper specifically locates this episode of English curriculum change in New Zealand in the context of larger debates of decolonising the curriculum.

journal_name: New Zealand Journal of Educational Studies
title: Sub-warden and Student Perspectives of Pastoral Care in University Colleges
abstract: Abstract Following the tragic undiscovered death of a student in a university college (or hall of residence) in New Zealand in 2019, a Pastoral Care Code was introduced to ensure the safety and well-being of students. Although much research has been conducted on pastoral care in higher education, little is known about pastoral care in colleges. Consequently, this research explored sub-warden and student perspectives of pastoral care and how it is implemented in colleges. A qualitative case study approach was conducted in colleges at the University of Otago, NZ. Data were collected through interviews and focus groups with six sub-wardens and nine students across six different colleges. Analysis was underpinned by Mason Durie’s Te Whare Tapa Whā wellbeing model, with themes developed using a general inductive approach. Key findings from the sub-wardens included not enacting a holistic approach to pastoral care, having difficulties setting professional boundaries, and desiring better training and support. journal_name: New Zealand Journal of Educational Studies
title: Decentering the Anglocentric Views on Literacy from a Multilingual and Multicultural Lens: A New Zealand Nuanced Perspective
abstract: Abstract In Anglophone nations, there appears to be a radical push to mandate the Science of Reading (SoR) or structured literacy into classrooms. While structured literacy appears to be cordial to a number of academics, popular media used this trend to generate discourses against other needs-based adaptations, suggesting that the science of literacy is already “settled” and can never be malleable. However, circumspective scholars of literacy and explicit instruction do not necessarily subscribe to this discourse, and they suggest a more nuanced understanding about the teaching of reading and writing in English especially when one realises that contemporary Anglophone classrooms are now rarely monolingual and monocultural. Using poststructuralist critical inquiry, this paper interrogates the dominant discourses around structured literacy policy and instruction that are often based on monolingual Anglophone bias. It problematises the inherent structures and assumptions of a “settled” science of reading instruction and unpacks the often marginalised worldviews and lived experiences of culturally and linguistically diverse learners which are strengths to leverage rather than deficits

journal_name: New Zealand Journal of Educational Studies
title: A Vision for Science Education in Aotearoa New Zealand: Discussions from a National Summit
abstract: Abstract Aotearoa New Zealand is in the midst of a curriculum update, with much attention focused on what the new draft science curriculum will look like after a 2023 draft resulted in much public discussion and was abandoned. To stimulate and support national conversation about key considerations of an inclusive, future-facing science curriculum, the Science Learning Hub Pokapū Akoranga Pūtaiao and Royal Society Te Apārangi hosted a one-day summit in July 2024. This paper reports on key themes emerging from roundtable conversations of participants in relation to the purpose of science education, important outcomes for science education, school science and curriculum design, and challenges and opportunities moving forward. The findings are salient in the current context of change.

title: Teachers’ Experiences of Curriculum Reform in Aotearoa New Zealand
abstract: Abstract New Zealand teachers have faced a period of significant curriculum reform over the past four years. With the government’s recent announcement of plans to reform the national qualification, and the proposal to introduce new subjects into the curriculum, we know more change is coming. This may result in role overload for teachers. Role overload occurs when the demands of a role surpass the time and resources available to an individual. Over recent decades, as teachers’ roles have evolved and expanded, evidence suggests there has been an increase in stress and burnout rates. This article reports on a small-scale study which explored the experiences of a group of early-adopter teachers attempting to enact Te Mātaiaho: The Refreshed New Zealand Curriculum (Ministry of Education in Te Mātaiaho: the refreshed New Zealand Curriculum: draft for testing, New Zealand Government, 2022), which was the first of several curriculum rewrites. The findings of the study shed light on the significant demands that complex curriculum reform places on teachers highlighting the emotional and professional toll this can take.
